target: AG1’s claim that AI is broadly beneficial because it increases convenience, health, accessibility, and workplace safety
objection: AI is not good for society overall because, even if it brings convenience, it also automates away jobs and harms small businesses, weakens critical thinking by encouraging people to outsource understanding, replicates and amplifies racism through biased data and deployment, and creates serious privacy risks through large-scale data collection and sensitive inference. These harms are said to be built into AI deployment at scale, not fixed by simply saying it was “designed responsibly.”

target: AG2’s claim that AI’s harms make it not good for society and that safeguards are insufficient
objection: AG2 is treating governance as either perfect or useless. In reality, regulation, independent evaluation, transparency requirements, phased rollouts, and liability can reduce AI harms enough to make responsible deployment feasible. AI can be deployed with safeguards that preserve benefits such as productivity gains, reskilling, accessibility tools, and safety improvements.

target: AG1’s claim that safeguards like reskilling, tutoring design, auditing, anonymization, and on-device processing can solve the main problems
objection: Those safeguards are structurally unlikely to be implemented well at scale, and even when present they do not remove the core harms. Profit incentives and speed mean workers still bear transition costs, “tutoring” still encourages shortcut behavior and reduced reasoning practice, audits do not eliminate bias baked into data and objectives, and privacy risks remain because systems can infer sensitive information from large-scale data and outputs.

target: AG2’s claim that because safeguards are imperfect, AI is not good for society overall
objection: That conclusion overstates the case because it assumes governance must be perfect to matter. Real-world mechanisms such as enforceable regulation, independent audits, transparency rules, phased rollouts, and liability can materially change incentives and reduce harm. The existence of remaining risk does not negate AI’s positive effects for accessibility, health, and workplace safety.

target: AG1’s claim that governance can make AI responsible through regulation, transparency, phased rollouts, and liability
objection: AI harms are hard to measure and control because models are opaque, frequently updated, and controlled by private firms that do not fully disclose data or internal mechanisms. Many harms—job pressure, subtle bias, privacy leakage through inference—occur broadly and incrementally rather than at a single identifiable point of failure, so safeguards are reactive, uneven, and unable to keep up with deployment at scale.

target: AG2’s claim that opacity, frequent updates, and private ownership make AI governance too hard to justify net-positive deployment
objection: Those difficulties do not prove AI is not good for society overall. Safeguards can be built for exactly those conditions, such as continuous monitoring, post-deployment evaluation, red-teaming, standardized model documentation, and privacy-preserving methods like differential privacy or federated approaches. AI benefits such as accessibility and health/safety support can still be delivered in limited, supervised settings, making net-positive outcomes plausible.

target: AG1’s claim that continuous monitoring, red-teaming, documentation, and privacy techniques can manage AI risk at scale
objection: Those safeguards may work in narrow pilots, but they do not solve the scaling problem. Continuous monitoring requires ongoing data collection that recreates surveillance/privacy harms, red-teaming cannot enumerate every emergent failure mode in constantly updated systems, and AI can flood the environment with fluent but false or manipulative content that erodes critical thinking and intensifies abuse toward racial minorities.

target: AG2’s claim that scale makes AI harms overwhelming and governance ineffective
objection: The same scale that amplifies harms also makes AI useful for defense. AI can detect spam, scams, fraud, deepfakes, impersonation, and other abuse; privacy-preserving monitoring can limit surveillance; and enforceable constraints such as approval requirements, incident reporting, rollback procedures, and content provenance standards can meaningfully reduce risk without foreseeing every possible failure.

target: AG1’s claim that AI-based defenses and provenance tools can mitigate AI harms at scale
objection: Those defenses create new harms and still do not stop the core pattern. Automated moderation and fraud detection are not neutral and can disproportionately suppress racial minorities, dissenters, or small creators, turning mitigation into censorship or discrimination. Watermarking and provenance are also fragile and uneven across platforms, so AI-to-fight-AI becomes an arms race with biased chokepoints and unreliable enforcement.
